findings.stat_label: non-network ATM fee, yours vs peer median
findings.headline: Your non-network ATM fee is well above the market range.
findings.body: At $4.50, it is 2.3× the $2 peer median and the 86th percentile of 21 peers (middle half of the market: $1–$2.50). It recurs for every customer who banks outside your ATM footprint.

findings.headline: Several lines are priced below the market.
findings.body: Your NSF / returned-item fee ($20 vs a $27.75 median) and overdraft fee ($20 vs a $30 median) each sit below the peer 25th percentile. Below-market returned-item pricing is a position many institutions are moving toward. If the pricing is deliberate, it is worth stating plainly in account marketing.

findings.stat_label: deposited-item return fee, yours vs peer median
findings.headline: Your deposited-item return fee is above the market range.
findings.body: At $35, it is $10 above the $25 peer median and the 96th percentile of 26 peers (middle half of the market: $15–$30). This fee falls on the depositor for a check someone else wrote, which makes it a frequent example in fee-fairness criticism.

exec_narrative: First Credit Union is compared with 141 credit unions under $10B in assets nationwide that publish fee schedules in the Bank Fee Index. The size band is wider than usual because fewer than 40 credit unions in your own size tier have published data; local competitors may price differently. Of 9 rankable lines, five sit inside the middle half of the market, two above it (non-network ATM fee and deposited-item return fee), and two below it (NSF / returned-item fee and overdraft fee). We would suggest two steps, in order of value: (1) review the non-network ATM fee, which sits well above the market range; the peer median of $2 is the reference point; (2) state the below-market NSF / returned-item fee in account marketing, where peers' published schedules make it verifiable.

callouts.title: Non-network ATM fee — $4.50
callouts.stat: Peer median $2 · middle half $1–$2.50 · range $0.50–$10 · 86th percentile · n=21
callouts.body: Published as “Out-of-Network ATM Usage.” At $4.50 it is 2.3× the $2 peer median. It recurs for every customer who banks outside your ATM footprint. Holding the premium is reasonable if the service behind it is differentiated; otherwise the peer median of $2 is the reference point.

callouts.title: Deposited-item return fee — $35
callouts.stat: Peer median $25 · middle half $15–$30 · range $5–$40 · 96th percentile · n=26
callouts.body: Published as “Deposit Item Returned for NSF.” At $35 it is $10 above the $25 peer median. This fee falls on the depositor for a check someone else wrote, which makes it a frequent example in fee-fairness criticism. A penalty fee offers little service to differentiate on, so the peer median of $25 is the natural reference point.

callouts.title: NSF / returned-item fee — $20
callouts.stat: Peer median $27.75 · middle half $23–$30 · 25th percentile · n=60
callouts.body: Published as “Non-Sufficient Funds - Overdraft.” Below-market returned-item pricing is a position many institutions are moving toward. If it is a deliberate choice, it belongs in account marketing; if it is an old price that was never revisited, the median of $27.75 is the reference point.

callouts.title: Overdraft fee — $20
callouts.stat: Peer median $30 · middle half $22.50–$34 · 26th percentile · n=31
callouts.body: Published as “Overdraft Payment Service.” A below-market overdraft fee is a claim peers' own published schedules can substantiate. If it is a deliberate choice, it belongs in account marketing; if it is an old price that was never revisited, the median of $30 is the reference point.

context_narrative:
Overdraft and returned-item fees have been the focus of regulatory and public attention since 2022, and many of the largest banks have reduced overdraft fees or eliminated NSF fees outright. Community institutions have moved more slowly and more unevenly, which is why the spread inside a peer set is often wider than the headline national averages suggest.

Fee schedules are also now public in a practical sense: they are collected, compared and summarized automatically. A customer or examiner comparing First Credit Union with its peers sees the same published lines this report uses, so the schedule is a positioning document as much as a pricing one.

How to use this report: § 02 shows every line against the peer range; § 03 explains the lines that sit outside it; § 05 names peers line by line. Ranked comparisons require at least eight peers publishing the same line. Where your institution offers several amounts for one category, the report uses the standard consumer charge described in the methodology below.
